newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Protests cast shadow over Hong Kong handover.
newsitem.headline: Protests cast shadow over Hong Kong handover.

text.p: Hong Kong's pro-democracy movement kept up pressure on Chinese authorities on Wednesday, staging a protest and vowing to mar elaborate ceremonies to mark the British colony's handover to Communist China on June 30.

A dozen shouting protesters, angered by what they said were signs of Chinese troops acting above the law, marched on the central Hong Kong base where advance units of the People's Liberation Army (PLA) are billeted.
The protesters said the PLA garrison in Hong Kong had been given special customs privileges at the border and this boded ill for their behaviour and rights in future.
China moved quickly to play down the incident, saying it had stemmed from a misunderstanding caused by language problems at a main border crossing.
But members of Hong Kong's elected colonial legislature, which will be dismissed during the handover ceremonies, will have talks with government officials this week to highlight the row over the PLA.
Hong Kong residents have vivid memories of the PLA crushing the pro-democracy movement centred in Beijing's Tiananmen Square in June 1989.

Perhaps no aspect of the handover has raised more concern in Hong Kong than the arrival of PLA troops. An advance group of about 200 PLA soldiers has already moved in and an undisclosed number will cross the border in the early hours of July 1.

Protests, rows and repeated threats by pro-democracy leaders to disrupt the handover are certain to have upset China, which is sending its senior leadership to the festivities and has been counting on a carefully orchestrated ceremony.
China has called the handover celebrations the media event of the century. Prince Charles will hand back Hong Kong, after 156 years of British rule, to China's President Jiang Zemin.
The heir to the British throne will then set off aboard the royal yacht Britannia after surrendering his country's last colony in Asia.

Pro-democracy leaders, determined to keep freedoms granted in the twilight of British rule, have raised the pressure in the final days, vowing to occupy the colonial parliament on handover night to protest against the disbanding of the elected assembly.
"I'm really afraid (if) something goes wrong at this time," said Bob Broadfoot, who manages the think-tank Political and Economic Risk Consultancy.
"That would be such a bad thing for Hong Kong right now ... If something like that happens, fingers will point and everyone will be blaming everyone else," he said.

But the Democratic Party, largest in the doomed assembly, repeated on Wednesday that it would occupy the building and read out statements while China's new, hand-picked legislature is being sworn in at a downtown convention centre.
China has been at pains to reassure Hong Kong's 6.4 million residents, and wary Western governments, that its "one country, two systems" policy will be strictly applied after the handover.

In Beijing, China claimed credit for Hong Kong's prosperity and stability, saying its decision not to invade after sweeping to power on the mainland in 1949 was a crucial factor in the colony's present wealth and thriving capitalist system.

In a front-page story, the official People's Daily said China has been a "strong backup" to Hong Kong, providing the territory ceded to Britain after the 19th century opium wars with food and water for decades.
